what_happened: The user corrected Athena's second reading of a request in job p806. The reading treated a refusal message as something addressed to an operator. The user said the refusal is for whoever runs Athena, so it should not be worded for an operator. The reading was corrected before the work went on.
cause: Athena builds readings from inside its own operating model, where the person who handles problems is the "operator". Nothing requires a reading to name who will see a user-facing message or output and what that person knows. The default internal vocabulary leaks into the wording of deliverables. A reading with the wrong reader is accepted, and only the user's correction exposes it. This is not an ambiguous verb or a missing finding from an earlier job. The reading was wrong about who the output is for.
prevention: Make the reading template require an explicit "audience" field for every message, refusal, error or document the job produces. The field names the reader and their role (for example, whoever runs Athena, not an operator). It is checked against a short glossary of reader roles kept in the defaults. Any acceptance criterion about wording must state that audience. The verifier then checks the produced text against the named audience, not against internal terms.
proposed_request: In job p806's work, make the refusal message that Athena shows when it refuses a request written for whoever runs Athena, not for an operator. Use plain words that do not assume knowledge of Athena's internal operator workflow. State what was refused, why, and what the person can do next. Also change the reading step so each reading names the audience of every message or output the job produces, and add a check that the produced text matches that named audience. Acceptance: the refusal text contains no operator-only instructions or internal jargon, and a test shows the reading records an audience for each user-facing message.
